notes: Packet timestamps are the kernel's receive times, and start_ns/end_ns, closed_at_ns, eval_start_ns and eval_end_ns are all on the same wall clock. eval_end_ns - end_ns is the detection delay after the window ended; it includes the grace period the detector waits for late packets before closing a quiet window. eval_end_ns - eval_start_ns is the processing time per window. Detection latency from attack start is eval_end_ns of the first flagged window minus the attack start.

heap_alloc_bytes, user_cpu_ns, sys_cpu_ns, cpu_interval_ns and cpu_share describe the detector process itself, sampled once per window right after the window is evaluated. The CPU columns cover the wall-clock interval since the previous sample (cpu_interval_ns) and are summed over all threads; cpu_share is (user + sys) / interval, where 1.0 is one core fully busy. In a live capture the interval is about one window length. In a trace replay the input is read as fast as possible, so cpu_share is close to 1 by construction; use (user_cpu_ns + sys_cpu_ns) / packets as the cost per packet instead. sys_cpu_ns is mostly the capture's system calls. On Linux the user/sys split has a resolution of one scheduler tick.

host_busy_ns, host_total_ns, host_softirq_ns and host_max_core_share describe the CPU use of the whole machine, read from /proc/stat at the same moments as the detector's own CPU columns. They include the packet processing the kernel does in softirq, which the process's own columns miss, and everything else running on the machine, such as memwatch, so the sender should run on another machine. host_total_ns is all CPU time over the interval summed over the cores, idle included, about cpu_interval_ns times the number of cores; host_busy_ns / host_total_ns is the share of the whole machine in use. host_softirq_ns is the part of host_busy_ns spent in softirq. host_max_core_share is the busy share of the busiest core: packets are processed on the cores that receive them, so one core can be saturated while the machine is not. /proc/stat counts in 10 ms ticks per core. The cost of the detector itself is host_busy_ns minus that of a baseline run with the same traffic and no detector.

The number of packets sent is not recorded here: the detector only sees what arrives. Save the tcpreplay output from the sender next to this run.json; together with live.socket and live.nic_delta it shows how many packets were lost before the detector and at which layer.

Sources flagged by their per-IP verdict were added to the blocklist of blocklist.c, an XDP program on the interface, which dropped their packets before they reached the capture socket. Dropped packets are not in packets/bytes, kernel_drops or live.socket, nor in any count the thresholds see; they are in blocked_packets/blocked_bytes. Unlike the kernel-space detector's, these are counted when a window closes, not by the time of the dropped packet: a window's figure is what was dropped since the previous window closed, including the grace period after the window's end. blocked_at_ns - end_ns is the delay from the end of the window to the sources being blocked. A source stays blocked for block_ttl after it was last flagged (0: until the run ends); when the blocklist is full, the source XDP saw last in the oldest window is evicted, the one with the fewest drops among equals. The blocklist is cleared when the run starts but not when it ends.

bpf_memory is the kernel memory of the XDP blocklist's maps, each as the kernel reports it (memlock in the map's fdinfo: computed per map type from Linux 6.4 on, estimated from the map's dimensions before). The maps are charged to the memory cgroup of the process that loaded blocklist.o (ip link), not to the detector's, so memwatch's main for the detector does not include them. Both maps are per-CPU, grow with the number of possible CPUs, and are preallocated, so their memory does not depend on the traffic. The program itself, its instructions and JIT image, is not included.

methods.flood: Centered median of nine consecutive counted windows >10,000 packets; cutpoints are starts of first and last qualifying windows; half-open interval. For blocking runs, use counted + blocked + socket drops to locate the flood.
methods.phase_origin: First recorded window start_ns, not process launch; matches the Pi source's reported phase times.
methods.cpu: Ratios of summed contemporaneous windows.csv counters. Host percentages use host_total_ns; process uses cpu_interval_ns. CPU per counted packet includes all host busy time.
methods.latency: evaluated=true and detector warm_up=false, using integer timestamp differences; distinct from evaluator's 75-window exclusion.
methods.memory: Sample median main plus stable, separately charged BPF maps; no program/JIT memory.
methods.blocking: Block events are new admissions from stats.blocklist.blocked, excluding refreshes; unique sources from successful ips.csv updates.
